attestations.notes: Steps 1.1–4.1 use a nonempty first-order domain, Separation with z != z, and Extensionality; existence does not assume an empty-set axiom.
Steps 1.1–4.1 choose one member B of nonempty x, separate inside B, and prove the defining universal membership condition independent of B; the empty family is excluded.
Steps 1.1–4.1 separate precisely the subsets from the containing set supplied by Power Set; Extensionality proves uniqueness, also for empty x.
Steps 1.1–2.1 expand membership in empty, singleton and pair families; intersection is applied only to nonempty singleton/pair families, including a=b.
Steps 1.1–3.1 show {a} and {a,b} lie in P(A union B), hence the Kuratowski pair lies in its power set; empty factors give no assumed elements.
Steps 1.1–4.1 check both implications and exhaust a=b and a!=b; singleton degeneration yields a=c=d.
Steps 1.1–4.1 apply unordered-pair equality to the two Kuratowski pairs; both matched and swapped singleton cases force equality of both coordinates.
Steps 1.1–3.1 bound both coordinates of every pair in R by union union R, then use Separation; the empty relation gives empty coordinate sets.
Steps 1.1–3.1 separate in one inductive I0 using quantification over all inductive sets, prove successor closure and leastness, then mutual inclusion proves uniqueness.
Steps 1.1–5.1 identify S as inductive and use leastness of omega; the property version uses Separation on N and the converse uses membership as its predicate.
Steps 1.1–3.1 induct on simultaneous transitivity and irreflexivity; either alternative sigma(n) in n or sigma(n)=n contradicts n notin n.

Steps 1.1–6.1 intersect closed relations, prove totality by P3, and remove an offending base/successor pair; P1 prevents a base deletion and P2 plus unique predecessor value preserves closure. Uniqueness follows by induction.
Steps 1.1–2.1 derive P1 from the member n of sigma(n), P2 from transitivity and no self-membership, and P3 from induction; no recursion assumption is needed.
Steps 1.1–3.1 apply Peano recursion with initial m and transition sigma; the unique functions define a total addition with the exact stated second-variable recursion.
Steps 1.1–3.1 induct on c, with base c=0 and successor recursion on both parenthesizations; a and b remain arbitrary.
Steps 1.1–3.1 induct on n to establish left zero identity; the right identity is the defining recursion clause.
Steps 1.1–3.1 induct on the second argument, moving the successor by the defining right recursion; the two successor applications agree.
Steps 1.1–3.1 induct on n using left identity for the base and left-successor compatibility for the step; no commutativity is assumed in either supplier.
Steps 1.1–3.1 induct on the common right summand k and use successor injectivity; the induction hypothesis quantifies over both m and n.
Steps 1.1–3.1 the set of zero or successors contains zero and every successor, so induction exhausts N; the nonzero conclusion discards the zero alternative.
Steps 1.1–3.1 exclude opposing strict relations by cancellative addition and nonzero successors; induction on n proves comparability, including the predecessor case when m>n.
Steps 1.1–3.1 give reflexivity and transitivity by additive witnesses, totality by trichotomy, and antisymmetry by cancellation and the zero-sum consequence of P1.

Steps 1.1–2.1 turn a nonzero additive witness into its predecessor and use successor compatibility; reverse implication excludes equality by cancellation and P1. The immediate-successor conclusion follows.
Steps 1.1–2.1 use pair coordinate uniqueness for the forward product criterion and domain/range witnesses for its converse; all inclusions hold for empty R.
Steps 1.1–2.1 bound inverse and composite pairs in the reversed and composite coordinate products and separate there; restrictions separate in R. Empty relations cause no existential witnesses.
Steps 1.1–3.1 establish zero != sigma(0) by P1 and propagate through successor injectivity; induction rules out every fixed point.

Steps 1.1–6.1 first prove N transitive; mixed order transitivity and discreteness yield m<sigma(n) iff m<=n. Two inductions identify membership with strict order; irreflexivity then proves inclusion iff nonstrict order.

Steps 1.1–7.1 normalize an injection by a codomain transposition and restrict it to obtain the forbidden smaller injection; zero base and transposition degeneracy are handled. Restriction and inverses yield all four consequences without a choice principle.

Steps 1.1–3.1 assuming no least element, induct on the initial segments avoiding S; the successor implication uses discreteness and injectivity. All N avoiding S contradicts its stipulated nonemptiness.
Steps 1.1–3.1 recurse from zero with transition x -> x+m, a total function on N; uniqueness defines total multiplication with the exact right-successor clause.
Steps 1.1–2.1 transport an additive witness and cancel the common translation for the converse; cancellation also preserves strict inequality in both directions.
Steps 1.1–3.1 use the right recursion for n*1 and simultaneous induction for 0*n and 1*n, including the zero base.

Steps 1.1–3.1 induct on c for distributivity and independently on n for the left-successor law; the latter uses only associative and commutative addition, avoiding circular multiplication commutativity.
Steps 1.1–3.1 induct on the second variable, with left-zero base and the established left-successor law matching the right recursion.
Steps 1.1–3.1 induct on c; the successor expansion uses left distributivity to combine a*(b*c)+a*b.
Steps 1.1–4.1 express both nonzero naturals as successors; right recursion makes the product a successor, so P1 excludes zero.
Steps 1.1–2.1 distribute an additive order gap through multiplication; strictness requires both the gap and k nonzero, then no zero divisors and additive cancellation.
Steps 1.1–4.1 add the two defining representative equations and regroup to obtain the addition equivalence; swapping coordinates yields negation equivalence.

Steps 1.1–5.1 establish equivalence when the first representative changes by factoring both sides through a+bprime=b+aprime; symmetry handles the second factor, and transitivity gives both replacements.
Steps 1.1–2.1 verify each ring axiom on representatives; expanded multiplication coordinates agree under associativity/distributivity and the swapped pair supplies the additive inverse.
Steps 1.1–5.1 use natural translation invariance to transport order across representatives; nonzero natural gaps in two positive integer representatives produce the positive product gap km.
Steps 1.1–4.1 distribute (0+0)*a and cancel one additive summand; this includes a=0.
Steps 1.1–3.1 differences of translated endpoints agree and differences of summed inequalities add in the positive cone; both conclusions use the exact cone axioms.
Steps 1.1–4.1 distribute additive inverse sums and identify inverses by uniqueness; double negation gives the two-negative product, including zero arguments.

Steps 1.1–4.1 positive-cone closure and negation identities give sign products and forward scaling; trichotomy rules out equality and the opposite strict order for both converses. Zero scaling is excluded.
Steps 1.1–3.1 split the nonzero element into positive or negative by trichotomy; cone multiplication and (-a)^2=a^2 prove positivity in both cases.
Steps 1.1–3.1 apply nonzero-square positivity to the field identity 1; the field hypothesis 1!=0 is essential.
Steps 1.1–5.1 a positive element has a nonzero inverse; a negative inverse would contradict 1>0. Multiplication by the positive product of two inverses reverses their order.
Steps 1.1–2.1 compare two additive identities/inverses using associativity and commutativity, then repeat in the multiplicative group of nonzero elements; inverse notation is restricted to x!=0.
Steps 1.1–3.1 exhaust all sign patterns for nonzero integers using ordered-ring positivity and negation; cancellation follows from (x-y)z=0 with z!=0.
Steps 1.1–3.1 multiply the representative cross-equations to verify product, sum and negation equivalence; denominator products are nonzero in Z by the earlier cancellation supplier.
Steps 1.1–2.1 check ring identities on nonzero-denominator representatives and scale/cancel the common factor in distributivity; nonzero numerator permits the reciprocal pair (b,a).

Steps 1.1–4.1 keep all denominators positive; positive integer scaling transports cross-product order across representatives and yields transitivity and addition compatibility. Positive numerators multiply positively.
Steps 1.1–4.1 evaluate e*f using its left and right identity equations; the consequences compare each one-sided identity with the available two-sided one, without associativity.

Steps 1.1–4.1 compare h*(g*hprime) and (h*g)*hprime using monoid associativity; both one-sided inverses coincide and are two-sided. Identifying a single one-sided inverse requires g already invertible.
Steps 1.1–3.1 induct from 1>0 for positive embedded naturals, iterate the positive successor gap for injectivity, and use separate addition/multiplication inductions for both arithmetic identities.
Steps 1.1–2.1 the equivalence relation makes [(m,0)]=[(n,0)] iff m=n; representative arithmetic preserves operations/order and a nonnegative gap a=b+k identifies every nonnegative integer uniquely.
